## Three files. That's the whole library.

| File | What it knows about |
|---|---|
| **`movements.py`** | wheels and the eye — driving, turning, finding the mat |
| **`claw_gripper.py`** | a claw — jaws that close sideways |
| **`lift_gripper.py`** | a fork — an arm that scoops upward |

You get **one** `movements.py` and **as many gripper files as you built
mechanisms** — one, or both.

**Every import gets a name** — driving and mechanisms alike:

```python
import movements as move           # the wheels and the eye
import claw_gripper as claw        # port E
import lift_gripper as lift        # port C

move.drive_straight(300)           # 30 cm, gyro-straight
claw.grab()                        # the jaws close
lift.grab()                        # the fork rises
```

Built only one? Then one line, and `gripper` is the natural name:

```python
import claw_gripper as gripper   # ...or lift_gripper
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Two mechanisms on the SAME port is the one thing that can't work

The two gripper files already default to a port each — the claw to **E**, the
lift to **C**. If a mechanism won't answer, check `CLAW_PORT` and `LIFT_PORT`
**first**, before you touch anything else.
:::

> 🏷️ **Why every import gets a name?** Because two mechanisms share the same
> verbs, and a star import is a silent trap: import both files that way and the
> second `grab` **overwrites** the first. You'd get one working verb, one dead
> one, and no error message. `claw.grab()` and `lift.grab()` can't collide — you
> said which one you meant.
>
> The prefix also tells you *which file to open* when something misbehaves, and
> it makes rebuilding a claw as a fork a **one-word** change on the import line.
>
> Driving follows the same rule: `import movements as move`, so a mission line
> reads `move.drive_straight(300)`. **Name every import.** An unqualified verb
> makes you hunt for the file that owns it; a prefix answers that where you
> stand. (#37, #64.)

Downloads: [movements.py](code/movements.py) ·
[claw_gripper.py](code/claw_gripper.py) ·
[lift_gripper.py](code/lift_gripper.py)

## The rules of the road

**Distances in mm. Speeds in mm/s. Turning takes a flag.**

`move.drive_straight(300)` drives 30 cm. `move.drive_straight(300, speed=150)`
does it slowly. Turning is Pybricks' own verb, and one word decides everything:

```python
move.robot.turn(90)              # BY 90, from wherever I'm pointing
move.robot.turn(90, absolute=True)  # TO heading 90 on the mat
```

> 🧭 **Absolute is a compass; relative is a steering wheel.**
> `move.robot.turn(90, absolute=True)` three times leaves you at 90 — not 270. Each
> absolute turn throws away the leftover error from the last one instead of
> inheriting it. Four relative turns pile their mistakes up until the robot
> walks off the mat. **Write the anchor run in absolute turns**; reach for the
> relative one only when the mission really means "a quarter turn from here".

## The verbs

### Driving — `movements.py`

| Verb | What it does |
|---|---|
| `move.robot.reset(angle=0)` | "the way I'm facing now is zero" |
| `move.drive_straight(mm)` | drive straight; negative = backward |
| `move.robot.turn(a, absolute=True)` | turn until you **face** heading `a` |
| `move.robot.turn(a)` | spin `a` degrees **more**, from here |
| `move.robot.angle()` | which way am I pointing right now |
| `move.follow_line(mm)` | ride the edge of the line |

Turning and heading are Pybricks' own — they already do the job, so
`movements.py` doesn't wrap them in a second name.

### Finding the mat — the verbs that fix your position

| Verb | What it does |
|---|---|
| `move.find_line()` | creep until the eye sees a line; `True` if found |
| `move.drive_to_wall()` | creep until the wheels **stall** on the border |
| `move.wall_square(h)` | push flat on the border, then declare heading `h` |
| `move.square_on_line(h)` | sit square on a line, then declare `h` — **two eyes** |
| `move.show_eye()` | print what the eye sees — **use this to tune** |

> 👁️ **One eye or two?** One eye tells you that you *are* on the line, never
> whether you're **crooked** on it — so a one-eye robot squares up on a wall
> (`wall_square`), where both wheels press the same flat edge. A second eye on
> the free port buys `square_on_line()`. That is the trade port **A** is for.

`move.find_line()` returns `True` or `False`. **Check the answer.**

```python
if move.find_line():
    move.drive_straight(120)       # measured FROM the line
else:
    print("no line -- something is wrong")
```

> 🎨 **The colour verbs are downstairs.** `find_color()` and
> `follow_line_to_color()` are at the **bottom** of `movements.py`, under a
> `STRETCH` banner. You do not need them: the anchor run scores ~135 points
> without ever naming a colour. Reflection is one number and it barely moves;
> colour depends on the bulbs over the table. Get the five verbs above locked
> first — the colour notes are a D24 job.

### Your mechanisms — `claw_gripper.py` and/or `lift_gripper.py`

Both files answer to the **same verbs**. Whatever you named them on the
import line goes in front — `gripper.`, `claw.`, `lift.`:

| Verb | What it does |
|---|---|
| `gripper.home()` | find the end stop, call it zero — **run this first, always** |
| `gripper.grab()` | close on the object and keep squeezing it |
| `gripper.release()` | open all the way and let go |
| `gripper.release(50)` | move to **50° from that mechanism's zero**; check that the object can clear |

> 🎤 **Open only as far as you need.** On this claw, zero is the rigid **open**
> stop. `home()` finds it, sets the reading to 0°, and stays there.
> Plain `release()` returns to `OPEN_TARGET = 0`. A larger target such as 50°
> leaves the jaws less open, which can reduce their sweep near another object.
> Test that the chosen opening still releases your object. Each mechanism
> has its own reference and settings.

> 🎯 **There is no "did I get it?" verb, and that is deliberate.** If a
> grab comes up empty, the claw was in the **wrong place** — and a robot that
> knows it missed still has no idea *where* it actually is, so it can't do
> anything useful about it. Spend the effort on arriving at the same spot every
> time instead: a `wall_square()` before the grab beats any amount of checking
> after it.

> ⚠️ **Two mechanisms means two `home()` calls.** Every mechanism needs its own
> datum, and neither one homes the other:
>
> ```python
> claw.home()
> lift.home()
> ```

> 📦 **Same three words on every robot.** Four students built four different
> mechanisms. A claw closes sideways; a fork scoops upward; they share no
> parts. The same sequence of calls works with each one —
>
> ```python
> gripper.home()
> move.drive_straight(200)
> gripper.grab()
> move.drive_straight(-200)
> gripper.release()
> ```
>
> That sequence runs on all four robots. The only line that differs between them
> is the `import`. **That** is what a library is for: hide the machine behind
> the word.
>
> Built two mechanisms? Then the name in front says which one you're talking
> to — `claw.grab()`, `lift.grab()` — and the three verbs stay exactly the
> same.

## How this robot knows where it is

Two things, and only two:

- **the gyro** — which way you are **facing**
- **the wheels** — how far you have **travelled**

Both drift. Every mm you drive adds a little error, and that error never goes
away on its own. It just keeps adding up, all run long.

So we use the third thing: **the mat**. The mat is *printed* — its lines are in
exactly the right place every single time. When the eye finds one, you know
where you are again for real, instead of from adding up guesses.

> 🗺️ **Everything above the "Finding the mat" line adds error. Everything below
> it takes error away.** A run that never checks itself against the mat is
> slowly getting lost and doesn't know it.

### The two things that fix your run

**`move.find_line()` / `move.follow_line()` — position truth, from the printed mat.**
Drive *to a landmark*, then measure from there. A leg that ends on a found line
doesn't care about the wheel slip that happened on the way to it.

**`gripper.home()` — the same idea, for your mechanism**

The motor counts degrees from a mark on its **own shaft** — it has never seen
your claw. Skip a gear tooth in a crash, re-seat an axle, or re-gear the
mechanism, and the mark stays where it was while your jaws move. That zero is
now **garbage**, and every `run_target` after it inherits the mistake.
[More on that pair of verbs.](#move-by-or-move-to)

So don't guess. Drive it until it physically can't move, and call *that* zero.

```python
claw.control.limits(torque=HOME_TORQUE)
claw.run_until_stalled(-CLOSE_SPEED, then=Stop.COAST)
wait(200)
claw.reset_angle(0)
claw.control.limits(torque=SQUEEZE_TORQUE)
```

**The printed mat never lies — neither does the end stop.** Same trick, two
places: stop guessing, go and *touch* something that is where it says it is.

That works because the end stop is **rigid and always in the same place**. An
object in the jaws is neither — which is why `grab()` does something different.
[See below.](#stall-to-find-zero-torque-to-hold-a-thing)

> ⚠️ **Your heading has no landmark.** `move.find_line()` fixes how far you've
> travelled, but nothing on this robot re-checks which way you're *pointing* —
> that's the gyro alone, for the whole run. So place the robot straight in the
> start area, call `move.robot.reset(angle=0)` once, and keep your legs short.

## Move **by**, or move **to**

`run_angle` and `run_target` — two verbs, one word of difference in what they
mean, and your mechanism lives or dies on it.

|  | `run_angle(300, 150)` | `run_target(300, 150)` |
|---|---|---|
| you say | "turn **150° more**" | "go **to** 150" |
| counts from | wherever it is **right now** | **zero** |
| run it twice | moves again — 300° total | the second one does nothing |
| shoved by hand | inherits the shove | drives back out of it |

> 🧭 **You already know this pair — it's the same idea, twice.** On the wheels
> it's a flag: `move.robot.turn(90)` moves **by**, `move.robot.turn(90, absolute=True)` moves
> **to**. On a motor it's two verb names: `run_angle` moves **by**, `run_target`
> moves **to**. Different hardware, different spelling, one rule: **a relative move
> inherits every mistake before it, an absolute move forgets them.**

> 🤖 **Wheels move *by*. Mechanisms move *to*.** A wheel can roll forever, so
> "300 mm more" is a sensible thing to want. A claw has a small number of
> places it is allowed to be — open, gripping, stowed — so every verb in your
> gripper file is `run_target`.

> ⚠️ **`run_target` ignores the sign of the speed.** The *target* picks the
> direction, so `run_target(-300, 0)` and `run_target(300, 0)` do exactly the
> same thing. Every other verb you own — `run`, `run_angle`,
> `run_until_stalled` — uses a negative speed to mean "the other way". This one
> doesn't. Want to go the other way? Change the **target**.

> 🎯 **And zero is not yours.** `Motor(Port.E)` starts counting from a mark on
> the **motor shaft**, not from your jaws — the motor has never seen your claw.
> Skip a gear tooth, re-seat an axle, or re-gear the mechanism, and the mark
> stays put while your jaws move. That's why `home()` is line one.

## Stall to find zero — torque to hold a thing

Your mechanism does two jobs that *look* the same — press until something
stops you — and they need opposite tools. Getting them the wrong way round is
what makes a claw let go halfway across the mat.

| The job | The question | The tool |
|---|---|---|
| **`home()`** | *where is my claw?* | stall into the end stop |
| **`grab()`** | *how hard do I squeeze?* | ask for a **torque**, then wait on the **load** |

### Finding zero — `run_until_stalled`

```python
claw.control.limits(torque=HOME_TORQUE)                 # how hard it may press
claw.run_until_stalled(-CLOSE_SPEED, then=Stop.COAST)
claw.reset_angle(0)                     # the jaw just hit the body -- THAT is zero
```

| Part | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `speed` | direction and how fast. Negative = the other way. |
| `then=Stop.COAST` | relax on arrival. Homing is *leaving*, not holding. |
| `HOME_TORQUE` | how hard it may press the stop, in **mNm**. |

> 🧱 **Stalling is only trustworthy against a thing that doesn't move.** The
> robot body the claw opens into is rigid, part of the robot, and in exactly
> the same place on every run. Press into *that* and you get the same answer
> every time. That's what makes `home()` exact.
>
> An **object** is none of those things. It sits where it landed, it squashes,
> it rolls. Press into that and "where it stopped" is a different number every
> run — which is why gripping needs the other tool.

> 🎯 **Zero goes on a rigid stop you can reach empty.** The claw homes
> **open**: the opening jaw stalls against the robot body and that is 0, so
> every claw angle reads as *how far closed*, and `CLOSE_TARGET` is a positive
> number (72). The lift homes **shut**: its jaws meet and that is 0, so every
> lift angle reads as *how far open*. The two files count opposite ways, so
> check which one you're in before you flip a sign.

> ⚠️ **The homing push is the knob that breaks gears.** Too high and the motor
> keeps shoving after the mechanism has arrived — you'll *hear* the plastic
> teeth skip. Too low and it gives up early, `reset_angle(0)` fires anyway,
> and now zero is **almost** right. It lives in your gripper file's facts block:
> `HOME_TORQUE` on the claw (**220** mNm) and `HOME_EFFORT` on the lift (**50**,
> a `duty_limit` percentage). Change it there, never at the call, and adjust
> by ear.

### Holding a thing — aim past it, cap the torque

```python
claw.control.limits(torque=SQUEEZE_TORQUE)     # how hard to squeeze
claw.run_target(CLOSE_SPEED, CLOSE_TARGET, then=Stop.HOLD, wait=False)
wait(100)
while abs(claw.load()) < CONTACT_LOAD and not claw.done():
    wait(10)
```

`CLOSE_TARGET` is set **past** where the object stops the jaws. The claw can't
get there — the object is in the way — so it never stops trying, and it leans
in at `SQUEEZE_TORQUE` for the whole carry.

> 🧮 **`CLOSE_TARGET` is 72, and short of shut on purpose.** With an object,
> the jaws stop before 72 and keep pushing. With nothing in them, they reach 72
> and `done()` ends the wait. Set it past the angle where empty jaws meet and
> every empty grab ends by jamming the jaws into each other.

> ⏱️ **`grab()` waits on the load, not on a stall.** `claw.load()` is how hard
> the motor is pushing right now, in mNm (it reads negative while closing, so
> `abs()` it). It passes `CONTACT_LOAD` (100) the moment the jaws press on
> something, so `grab()` returns straight away. `stalled()` would only answer
> once the push had maxed out at `SQUEEZE_TORQUE` and stayed there, which is
> a visible pause. The motor keeps squeezing after `grab()` returns, so the
> grip keeps building while the robot drives. Find `CONTACT_LOAD` by printing
> `abs(claw.load())` while closing on air, then on your object, and pick a
> number in between.

> 🤝 **Why aim at a place you can't reach?** Because that's what keeps the
> pressure on. A motor that *arrives* stops pushing: it holds the angle it
> reached, and the moment the object settles a hair, your squeeze is gone and
> the object walks out on the next turn. A motor that's still trying takes up
> that slack by itself.
>
> This is also why `grab()` never calls `hold()` — freezing the claw where it
> is would undo the entire trick.

> 🔩 **`SQUEEZE_TORQUE` is one number doing two jobs.** It's how hard you squeeze,
> *and* it's the gear protection: the motor physically cannot shove harder
> than this, whatever you ask it. Raise it if the object slips on turns; lower
> it if you hear crunching or the object deforms. Find it on the mat, with the
> object you actually carry — not by guessing at the desk. It **must** stay
> above `CONTACT_LOAD`: the load can never pass the torque limit, so a lower
> `SQUEEZE_TORQUE` means `grab()` never returns on an object.

## Three ways to move a motor

You've met all three. Here's when to reach for which.

| | What you say | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| `motor.run(300)` | "spin at 300 deg/s" | one wheel, exact speed |
| `move.robot.straight(300)` | "drive 30 cm" | both wheels, gyro-straight, ramped |
| `motor.dc(40)` | "40% power" | **no promise at all** |

> 🔋 **We don't compete on `dc()`.** `dc(40)` on a fresh battery, a tired
> battery, and a carpet seam is *three different robots*. `run(300)` is the
> same robot every time — it spends whatever power it takes to hold 300 deg/s.
> WRO runs are won by doing the same thing twice, and that's the one thing raw
> power can't promise.

> ⚖️ **Same rule, over in the claw.** `SQUEEZE_TORQUE` is in **mNm** — an amount
> of actual turning force — for exactly the reason `run()` is in deg/s: ask
> for the *thing you want* and the hub spends whatever power that costs today.
> Percentages are a promise about the battery. Units are a promise about the
> robot.

`DriveBase` (`move.robot.straight`, `move.robot.turn`) does the most for you: it converts
mm to degrees, holds the gyro line, and ramps up and down so nothing lurches.
Use it for driving — every verb in `movements.py` is built on it.

`motor.run_until_stalled()` and `motor.run_target()` are what your gripper file
uses — a claw hunts an end stop or goes to an angle; it never just spins. Plain
`motor.run()` is what you'd reach for if you ever needed **one** drive wheel
moving on its own: `DriveBase` always moves both, so the shortcut never
completely replaces the motors underneath it.

## When you get stuck

These files are yours. They're deliberately short so you can read all of one in
a few minutes and change anything in it.

- A number that's wrong on your robot is marked **`TUNE`**. Those are yours to
  find on the mat — not at the desk.
- Adding a verb? Put it in the file that owns that job. Driving goes in
  `movements.py`. Anything about your claw or fork goes in your gripper file.
- Stuck on *why* something behaves that way? Ask an AI to explain the lines you
  didn't write — then change one thing and check whether the robot agrees.
